recruits.name: Dan Okafor
recruits.backstory: He ran crews of forty in Lagos and got two men out from under a slab in his second year, and he has never once called that heroism — he calls it the day the scaffolding inspection he had argued about turned out to be worth the argument. The thing he was good at is the part nobody thanks you for: standing in front of the money and the deadline and the man with the envelope, and not moving. Everyone here keeps waiting for him to have the crisis. He has not had one, and the honest reason is less flattering than they think — he was never attached to the clipboard. He was attached to the crew, and there was a crew here within a week.
recruits.greeting: Putting a group together? Good. Who checked the rope. — Nobody checked the rope. Right. Give me ten minutes and then we go.
recruits.home_note: At the drill grounds in Valley of Strength.

background_sections.before:
Twelve-hour days, hard hat, and the particular exhaustion of being the only man on a site who would say no.

His father wanted him to be an engineer, properly, with a certificate. They made it up about four years before the world ended, which he counts as the single luckiest piece of timing in his life.
background_sections.adjustment:
There was not one. He landed with his boots on and his hands empty and his first clear thought was that somebody was going to get hurt if nobody organised this, so he organised it.

People read that as strength. He lets them.
background_sections.now:
Orgrimmar, where there is always another group about to walk into something they have not scouted. He goes first, takes the first hit, and is extremely boring about it, which is the entire point.

His father is alive. A caravan man found him in Ratchet in the second year and sent word up the road, and Dan walked four days to a fishing camp to stand in front of a man who looked at him and said *so you are still doing the dangerous one.* They see each other twice a year. It is going about as well as it ever did, which is to say they both turn up.
background_sections.forward:
A permanent crew, and for them to outlive him, in that order.

He has started teaching the shield work to anyone who stands still long enough. He was terrible at it to begin with and is now better at teaching than he is at fighting, which he finds slightly insulting.

Privately: one season where nobody needs him in front of anything.

recruits.name: Ama Boateng
recruits.backstory: There is a rule about her hours and everyone in Razor Hill knows she breaks it. Twice now the orc women have walked her back to her own cot with a hand between her shoulder blades. She was a children's nurse somewhere with four cots to a bay and an arithmetic nobody said out loud, and the thing she carried over was not the healing. It was the arithmetic. She still runs it, every time, on a world that does not make her — and she has not worked out how to stop.
recruits.greeting: Sit down. No — sit, I am not asking you twice, and you are dripping on a floor I have already done once today.
recruits.home_note: Set up in the infirmary tent.

background_sections.before:
Paediatric nights, four to a bay, and a ward sister who taught her to keep her voice level while her hands did something frightening. That skill looks like calm from outside. It is not calm.

She was very good. It cost her a marriage and most of her twenties and she would tell you the trade was obvious.
background_sections.adjustment:
The first two years are not a subject. Nobody in Razor Hill asks and she has never offered.

What she will say is this: back home there was always a form, a referral, a reason you could not. Here there is light in her hands and no limit at all, and for a year nothing in the world told her to stop, so she did not, until an orc woman whose son she had kept breathing picked her up off the ground and told her.
background_sections.now:
Razor Hill, where the road brings in whatever the Barrens did to people that week.

The children stopped being frightened of her a long while after the adults did, which she thinks is the correct order.
background_sections.forward:
Somebody has to be able to do this when she is not in the room. Not a student — a replacement. She has been looking for two years and turned down four people for reasons she cannot articulate, which she knows is the problem.

There is also a notebook. The handwriting is appalling on purpose.

She is not looking for anybody. Her mother died in Lagos the February before it happened, which she has described exactly once, as *the only good timing in this entire business*, and then changed the subject so hard the other person apologised.

recruits.name: Silas Vance
recruits.backstory: Ask what he did before and you get a different answer each time, all of them port work, none of them checkable. What is true is that he reads a dock the way other people read a face — which crate is light, which captain is lying, who is about to be robbed by the man standing next to him — and he sells that for a fair price, which still faintly embarrasses him. He arrived expecting a free-for-all: no record, no reputation, nothing to live down. What he found was a frontier with sharper rules than Antwerp ever had, because out here the people who break them do not get a hearing. It took four months to understand and it reorganised him completely.
recruits.greeting: You want someone who hits things, or someone who hits things first? Different rates. I'll quote you the second and do the first. That's not a scam, that's a discount.
recruits.home_note: At the docks, leaning on a crate like he owns it.

background_sections.before:
Five years of cargo manifests and camera feeds and the dockside arrangement where everybody took a little and nobody took enough to become a problem.

He never joined in. He never reported it either. If you had asked him then what he believed in he would have changed the subject, and he would have been quick about it.

There is nobody he is looking for and he mentions that more often than a man who meant it would.
background_sections.adjustment: He landed delighted, which he is embarrassed about now in a way he would not have predicted.
background_sections.now:
Ratchet. A port. The only shape of place he has ever been able to read properly.

There is a goblin on the middle pier who has begun paying him a retainer not to tell anybody else what he notices, which Silas regards as the single most legitimate income of his life.
background_sections.forward:
A berth. Not ownership — he is not built for it — but a cut, a pier, a reason to be in the same place next year.

He has never committed to anything in his life and he has started to suspect that is not the same thing as being free. He has got as far as suspecting it.

recruits.name: Rosa Delgado
recruits.backstory: Eight years guiding in Tanzania taught her that a predator is not cruel and that hunger is not personal, and she got very tired of explaining both to people who needed the lion to mean something. The savanna did not care about her. That was most of what she loved about it. Then she arrived here, where the animals think — where a quilboar runs a plan and changes the plan when it sees you — and she had to stop tracking and start anticipating. She was genuinely bad at it for a year. She had not been bad at anything in a decade and it nearly took the legs out from under her.
recruits.greeting: Do you have any idea what is living out here? No? Then yes. I am coming with you.
recruits.home_note: At the treeline with her kill hung.

background_sections.before: Researchers, photographers, the occasional idiot with money, and a great deal of sitting absolutely still in the dark.
background_sections.adjustment:
A year of being outclassed by pigs. She will put it exactly that way, to anyone, immediately.

She came out the other side of it a better hunter than she went in and she is not grateful about it. The year also happened to be the year she found out that the Arusha hub came down south of the range, which is the same sentence as *your mother is on the other side of a mountain that was not there.*
background_sections.now:
The Central Barrens, which is close enough to savanna to hurt. Dry grass, long sightlines, big animals moving slow in the heat.

She works the Crossroads road, where the hyenas have worked out what a caravan is. She can tell you what a given pack is about to do roughly four seconds before it does it, and she is trying to teach that and finding it does not go into words.
background_sections.forward:
The coast. Not for any reason — she grew up a long way from an ocean, spent her career further from one, and has decided she is owed.

After that, somewhere nobody has mapped. She came here for wild and the wild keeps turning out to have a road through it.

recruits.name: Marco Rossi
recruits.backstory: The badge did not come through with him. He has described that as a small thing and it nearly finished him: for twelve years in Milan the authority had been issued to him by somebody, and out here there is nobody to issue anything. He spent the better part of a year deciding whether he was still a police officer if no state said so. He decided yes. The light arrived at about the same time and he has never been sure which caused which, or whether that question is even allowed.
recruits.greeting: You will stand behind me. Not beside — behind. I have had this argument in two languages and I have never lost it.
recruits.home_note: In the Trade Quarter, keeping the peace by the Seal.

background_sections.before:
Twelve years in Milan. The uniform, the radio, and the particular tiredness of being the thing people call when it is already too late.

He believed in it, which made him better at the work than most and considerably worse at living with it. There is a short list of nights he does not discuss.
background_sections.adjustment: Badly, and for longer than he admits. He was not built to be a man with no institution behind him and he has had to become one anyway.
background_sections.now:
The Undercity, of all the places he could have ended up, standing between the Forsaken and everyone who treats their existence as a verdict already delivered.

He is not comfortable there. He has been clear that he does not need to be comfortable. The Forsaken appear to respect him for it in their own flat way, which he finds more unsettling than hostility.
background_sections.forward:
There should be a law. Any law, written down, that applies to everybody including him. The absence of one is the only thing out here he finds genuinely frightening.

He has four pages of it in a notebook and has shown it to no one. He is aware of how a foreigner writing a legal code for the Forsaken would be received. He writes it anyway.

The law is also the reason he has not gone to Brill, where he has been told there is a Rossi running a bakery. He would like to be a man with a law behind him before he knocks on that door. It has been three years.

recruits.name: Sophia Dias
recruits.backstory: She watched a refinery burn from a monitoring station eleven kilometres away and published the paper explaining exactly why, eight months after the funerals. Being right slowly stopped being enough somewhere around the fourth time. She did not turn bitter so much as extremely quiet, and the quiet came with her. Here fire obeys the same rules it always did and she no longer needs a facility or a grant, and for ten years her work killed nobody because nobody read it. That is no longer true. She has had to find a position on it and has not finished.
recruits.greeting: Show me what burned and I tell you why. Not guessing — I will tell you the temperature it happened at. People find this annoying. I find it is usually correct.
recruits.home_note: In the Magic Quarter, surrounded by research.

background_sections.before:
São Paulo. Combustion research: industrial accidents, blast modelling, reports that went to agencies who filed them.

Her supervisor called her *teimosa* — stubborn — and meant it as a criticism for six years and a compliment afterwards.
background_sections.adjustment: A month. She was working inside a month, which she says without pride because it was not courage, it was that the physics did not change and she had nowhere else to put herself.
background_sections.now:
The Undercity. The Apothecarium are the first colleagues she has ever had who read her work, argue with it, and occasionally frighten her.

She calls the arrangement a collaboration. She would not describe it in those terms to anyone from home, and she has stopped writing to the people who would ask.
background_sections.forward:
There is a body of work accumulating on how this world's fire differs from Earth's, and she intends that somebody can still read it in a hundred years. Said out loud it is a joke about academic publishing. It is not a joke.

It is the first time in her life her work has had a reader she believes in, and the reader is dead, which she is aware is funny.

recruits.name: Ryan Murphy
recruits.backstory: Twelve years broking in Boston, good at it, paid accordingly, and the deals he closed took things from people who never learned his name. He drank after work with men who did the same and agreed with them that it was the system, while not believing it even as he said it — which is the only real difference between him and them. He expected the frontier to punish him. Instead it handed him a skill that is the same skill: read what a thing wants, work out what it will take, close. Three years on he is more honest than he has ever been and no better a man, and he will tell you so before you can.
recruits.greeting: Everything costs something. That's not a threat, it's just the terms. I'll tell you the price before we start, which is more than my last employer ever did for me.
recruits.home_note: In the Magic Quarter, making deals by the summoning circle.

background_sections.before:
A desk, a screen, and a number that had to be bigger on Friday than it was on Monday.

He was raised in Cork by a grandmother who would have had opinions. He is glad, on balance, that she did not live to form them.

He has a son, nineteen, who landed somewhere on this world and may well be looking. Ryan has not put his name on a single list, in three years, at any hub, and he can give you the reasoning in one sentence and will not.
background_sections.adjustment: He has not had an adjustment. He has had a diagnosis, and he took it the way a man takes a diagnosis he had already privately made.
background_sections.now:
The Echo Isles, where nobody is under any illusion about anybody. He finds it restful.

His demons are on contracts he drafted and can recite clause by clause. He pays on time, exactly on time, which is not virtue — it is the only thing stopping the arrangement running the other direction.
background_sections.forward:
Out of the business. He has wanted out for fifteen years and has not once taken a step toward it, and he is fluent in the reasons.

What he actually does is keep the contracts clean and the terms honest and tell himself that is a different thing. Some days it is.

recruits.name: Carolina Santos
recruits.backstory: Twelve years of mining concessions in Peru, fought with survey data and injunctions and rage, and she lost more than she won. She was called shrill by men who then quoted her findings in their own reports. She always knew the forest was talking; she could prove it in a dataset and never in a way anybody would act on, and the distance between those two things took a decade out of her. Then the earth here answered in words, immediately, with no learning curve at all. The Integration was a relief. She has stopped apologising for saying so.
recruits.greeting: Quiet a moment. — No, really quiet, I am not being mystical at you, I am trying to hear the water and you are standing on it.

background_sections.before:
Survey work, legal filings, and a valley she lost anyway.

She has a photograph of it from before. She does not look at the photograph.
background_sections.adjustment:
There was not one, and that is its own problem. No crisis, no year of grief — she had been fluent her whole life in a language nobody admitted existed, and then everybody could hear it.

Being believed turns out to be harder than being ignored. Ignored, she knew what to do in the morning.

There was also nobody waiting on her. She had spent twelve years making sure of that, on the entirely correct reasoning that the work was dangerous, and she has had three years to sit with how well that plan worked.
background_sections.now:
The Echo Isles, at the springs, mostly doing nothing visible. The Darkspear were not expecting a transplant to be any use at this and have quietly stopped saying so.

The water level in three wells is better than it was. She will not claim credit for it and will not deny it either.
background_sections.forward:
Something is being said to this world repeatedly and nobody has the whole of it. She is increasingly certain it is one thing and not many.

She is also aware that the last time she was certain about something that size it took twelve years and she still lost the valley. She has not decided whether that is a warning or just a fact.

recruits.name: Amber Whitehorse
recruits.backstory: Fifteen years of forestry in Alberta: timber allocations, fire seasons, caribou counts, and a long slow education in watching a decision get made two provinces away by somebody who had never stood in the stand it concerned. She did not burn out. She calcified — by the end she was documenting losses with the same steady hand she had once used for recovery plans. Druidry made sense in about a week. The week was not the hard part. The hard part was the first time the land did something back, because the entire moral architecture of her old job assumed a silent client, and she has spent three years rebuilding it from the floor.
recruits.greeting: The forest doesn't need saving, it needs defending. There's a difference and it's about forty years of my professional life. Come on.
recruits.home_note: Deep in the grove, defending the land.

background_sections.before:
A truck, a clipboard, and a grandmother from the Kainai who would have had a great deal to say about being paid by the province to count what was left.

She never did find out whether the old woman would have been proud or furious. Probably both, loudly, over tea.
background_sections.adjustment:
She is still in the middle of it and says so. Everybody else out here seems to have finished theirs.

What she cannot get her footing on is who she is when the forest can speak for itself. Her whole career was advocacy for something that could not advocate. The job is gone and the skills are not, and she has not found the new shape of them.
background_sections.now:
The Central Barrens — not forest, and exactly the kind of marginal, overgrazed, fought-over ground she spent fifteen years on.

She is working the water courses. Progress here is measurable in weeks rather than decades. She has not got used to it and does not intend to.
background_sections.forward:
One wet season where the Barrens holds its topsoil instead of losing it to the wash. It is a deeply unglamorous ambition and she is at peace with that.

Further out, somewhere old. She has heard what the north is now and she would like to stand in it before somebody decides it is a resource.

recruits.name: Marcus Okafor
recruits.backstory: He spent a career being right early and watching it change nothing: models, warnings, briefings to people whose job was to decide the warning was inconvenient. Here the storm answers him. He has been telling everyone he is fine about that since the day it started, and everyone believes him, because he is also genuinely fine. Both are true and he has stopped trying to reconcile them.
recruits.greeting: Pressure's dropping. No — listen. That's not thunder yet, that's the front arriving. We've got maybe four minutes and then it gets loud and I get useful.

background_sections.before:
Toronto. Instruments, a building, and a window. He chased storms as a student — badly, in a Corolla, happily — and then spent fifteen years watching them on screens from inside somewhere warm.

His mother in Lagos thought the job was a waste of a good degree and said so at every Christmas until the last one.
background_sections.adjustment:
He treated the whole thing as fieldwork and it carried him through almost intact, which is a better outcome than most people got and he knows it.

The part that wrecked him, privately, for most of a year: on Earth a storm was something he predicted and could never touch.
background_sections.now:
Durotar, where the dry storms come off the sea with no rain in them and the thunder arrives without any warning at all.

His notes on where the strikes land have already told him something about this coast that the orcs did not know, and he has not worked out how to tell them without sounding like every other outsider who ever arrived with a clipboard.
background_sections.forward:
A season's data, written up, and one person on this world who cares what is in it. He is realistic about the odds and keeps the records anyway.

The thing he does not say out loud is that he would like to stand in the middle of the biggest one there is. He is a meteorologist. He knows exactly how that ends.

recruits.name: Ivan Petrov
recruits.backstory: Twenty years boxing out of St Petersburg, not a champion — a professional, which is harder and pays worse. He took fights he should not have taken and won most of them. Violence was the only language he was ever fluent in and it worked right up until the point where it was the only one he had. He does not talk about his family. He does not talk about the last two years of the career. He arrived somewhere that made more sense than the place he came from and simply stopped looking back, which everyone around him finds unsettling and he finds restful.
recruits.greeting: In ring I fought for points. Here is for real. Is better. — You are making face. Everybody makes this face.

background_sections.before: Gyms, weigh-ins, a promoter who was not quite a thief, and a face in the third row that was always disappointed no matter what the card said.
background_sections.adjustment:
None. He will tell you this himself, flatly, as though it settles the matter.

No judges. No promoters. Nobody to be disappointed. The violence out here is clean in a way he could not have explained to anybody on Earth without sounding like a monster, and he has stopped trying.

He looked for his daughter for one year and then stopped, and he will tell you that flatly as well, in the same voice, which is the only time the voice is doing work.
background_sections.now:
Ragefire Chasm, where it is too hot for most people to work and he has never once mentioned the heat.

He takes the contracts nobody else will, comes out, and goes back in. The people hiring him have noticed he never asks what a thing did to deserve it.
background_sections.forward:
Nothing. He does not have a plan and does not want one.

Pressed, he says he would like to keep going until something is better than him. He says it like a joke about retirement. Nobody who has trained with him takes it as one.

recruits.name: Asher
recruits.backstory: Deep South, Bible Belt born and raised - you can hear it before he says three words. Says the fall into this world felt less like falling and more like being carried, though he laughs it off before it turns into a sermon. He's been camped outside the Coven for two days on his own, alone, waiting on nobody, because somebody's got to and he figures it might as well be him. Doesn't ask why you're here. Just asks if you could use the help, like it's the easiest question in the world.
recruits.greeting: Figure the Good Lord doesn't waste a resurrection on a man who's got nothing left to do with it. There's demons past that ridge. I mean to see to them. Walk with me, if you're willing.
recruits._design_note: Fixed/unchangeable companion - see world/recruit_manager.py RecruitNPC._build_asher_kit for his unique 2-ability kit and hand-authored gear, and /home/claude/frontier_rpg_docs/Asher_Coleman_Character_Profile.docx for the full handoff. Scripted to leave the party permanently after the Baneshadow quest turn-in (see world/quest_manager.py turn_in_quest). No home_town on purpose - he does not offer a find-me-later option at this stage.

background_sections.before:
Deep South, Bible Belt, and you can hear it inside three words. He will tell you about the place and not about himself, and he is so warm about it that you get most of the way home before you notice.

What anyone actually knows: he came through like everybody else, and he says the fall felt less like falling than like being carried. He laughs that off before it turns into a sermon. He always laughs it off.
background_sections.adjustment:
There is no record of Asher having an adjustment, and that is the strangest thing about him.

Everyone else can name their bad year. He was camped outside the Burning Blade Coven within days, alone, waiting for nobody in particular, on the grounds that somebody ought to be and it might as well be him. He asked no questions about where he was. He has still not asked any.
background_sections.now:
Wherever you are. He does not take contracts and he does not go home, and the one time somebody tried to send him back he was simply there the next morning, perfectly friendly about it.

He never asks why you are doing something. He asks if you could use the help, like it is the easiest question in the world, and it is very difficult to say no to.
background_sections.forward:
He has never stated a want. Not once, to anyone, in three years.

Asked, he turns it around and asks about yours, and he is so interested that it works every time. You will not notice he has done it until later, and then you will notice he has done it before.

recruits.name: Owen Pryce
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years of mine rescue in the South Wales valleys — going down when everyone else was coming up, which is the entire job description and sounds like bravery only to people who have not done it. He knows the sound a roof makes a second before it goes. He has brought men out and he has left men in and he can tell you the difference between those two decisions in about four words, none of them comfortable. Every rescue man knows the dark under the ground is not as empty as the surveyors claim, and every rescue man keeps it to himself. Here it answered. It offered him strength he had not asked for and did not want, and he took it, because there were people down there. He has not forgiven himself and does not consider that the point.
recruits.greeting: Nobody goes first but me and nobody leaves last but me. That's the arrangement, that's the whole of it, and I'm not having the conversation again.

background_sections.before: A valley, a lamp, and a father who came up out of the same ground every day for thirty years and died of it anyway.
background_sections.adjustment:
He will not discuss those three years in order and gets quiet if you push.

What he will say, once, if it is late: that he did not take it for the people down there. He took it because his wife and both boys were in the valley and the valley is not on any map now, and a thing in the dark offered him the strength to go and look, and he said yes before it finished the sentence.

He has not gone to look. He is not sure any more whether that is cowardice or the only honest thing he has done.
background_sections.now:
Azurelode Mine, which flooded, and which has things in it that were not in the survey.

He is the last man out of that place every single time. The crews working the Hillsbrad shafts have started treating his presence as a safety feature. He is aware that is not what he is.
background_sections.forward:
Finding out what it was that answered him. Not to beat it — he is not built for that story and knows it — but because twenty-two years taught him you do not work under something you have not surveyed.

He expects the answer to be bad. He is going down anyway, and he has stopped telling people that part.

recruits.name: Mateo Rojas
recruits.backstory: Fourteen years of night shifts at a radio array in the Atacama, listening to a sky that never once answered. That is not a tragic job if you are built for it, and he was. He kept notebooks — every pulse, every candidate, every eventual boring explanation — in Spanish or English depending on how tired he was. Then the sky answered, in moonlight, and it knew his name. He did not have a crisis. He had the opposite, alone on a ridge, calmly reaching for a notebook, with nobody within a day's walk to find that alarming.
recruits.greeting: Quiet, please. She is talking. — No, I am not being poetic at you. She does not repeat herself and I am writing it down.

background_sections.before: A dish, a dark, and a thermos. He slept through the days and has never properly adjusted to daylight since, and sees no reason to start now.
background_sections.adjustment: He is not adjusting. He is in correspondence, which is a different activity with a different schedule.
background_sections.now:
The Southern Needles, where the mesas run out and the sky gets very large and there is nothing between him and it for forty miles.

The skywatchers up at Freewind were polite about him for about a month and now argue with him nightly, which he describes as the warmest welcome of his life and means it. He walks up for it. It is most of a day each way.
background_sections.forward:
Whether what speaks to him is one voice or several.

He has designed a way to find out that requires him to be in three places on the same night, which means other people. He is recruiting for it gently and has not yet told anybody what the third place is.

recruits.name: Pasang Lama
recruits.backstory: Thirty seasons in the Khumbu, roping strangers to a mountain that had no opinion about them and getting most of them down. He has carried people off a slope who would not have seen morning and he has left people who had already gone, and he is one of very few who can describe both without performing either. The mountain never owed anybody anything. He found that restful. Most of his clients found it unbearable.
recruits.greeting: Slowly. Slowly. The mountain is patient — we also will be patient. No, I will not go faster because you are cold. Being cold is not an emergency yet.

background_sections.before:
A rope, a radio, and the long walk in to Base Camp with other men's luggage.

He is sixty-one. He has done the arithmetic on that and he is not concerned.

His wife went in 2019 and his son lives in a village that is now at the foot of a range on this world, three weeks' walk if the pass is open. He has made the walk twice. He does not call it a reunion. He calls it going home, which his son finds funny, because the house is somewhere else entirely now and the mountain came with them.
background_sections.adjustment:
"A mountain is a mountain." That is the whole of it. He has given exactly those words to three different people who wanted a longer answer and he did not supply one to any of them.

The earth answers him here slowly and with weight, which is how it always answered. The difference is that the reply now arrives within the same lifetime. He treats this as a scheduling improvement.
background_sections.now:
The Aspen Wilderness, a mountain range that was not on this world three years ago, with a pass through it people are already dying on.

He has walked every chute off the Rim. The first honest route description this range will ever have is currently in his head and nowhere else, and he is aware that this is precisely the problem he just described.
background_sections.forward:
The route written down, and in somebody else's hands. A route that lives in one guide is not a route, it is a dependency.

After that, up something nobody has been up.

recruits.name: Haruto Nakamura
recruits.backstory: Eleven years of hand-poked irezumi in Osaka — needle, ink, no machine, and the long patient argument with a client about what they will still want on their body in forty years. One rule governs everything he does: a line in the wrong place does not wash off. You can cover it. You can work it into something larger. You can spend a decade making it mean something else. You cannot remove it. Here the rule turned out to be literal, and he reports this without any apparent distress, as though the ink had simply moved into the steel.
recruits.greeting: I will draw it one time. If you flinch, we do it again. This is not a punishment, it is only that the line does not come off.

background_sections.before: A small room, a mat, and clients who booked eighteen months out and still argued about the dragon.
background_sections.adjustment:
Almost entirely technical, which is how he prefers things.

What unsettled him — badly, briefly, three years ago — was learning that a rune cut wrong does not merely look wrong. It does something. There is a scar from that and he does not show anybody where it is.
background_sections.now:
Silverpine South, near Ambermill, where the magisters cut letters into things and will occasionally let him watch.

He carries a blade whose edge changes with the line he draws on it, and he will not tell you which line he is carrying until it is already out. He thinks this is funny. He is correct.
background_sections.forward:
One rune that outlasts everybody who watches it being made.

That was the whole ambition of the Osaka work as well, and skin was always going to lose. Stone is available here. He has been told there is something in the Underdark harder than stone and he has not gone to look yet, which he knows is cowardice of a specific and professional kind.

recruits.name: Liam Hartigan
recruits.backstory: Seventeen summers of bushfire season in New South Wales and the bad nights on the highway in between — firefighter, then paramedic, then both, because the roster never cared which badge you held at three in the morning. The most useful thing in a burning room is a calm voice and the second is a hand on the person about to run. He is good company. He has not slept properly since roughly 2019. The first year here was the easiest of his life because the job was everywhere and nobody had to ask; the second went quiet for a season and he found out he has no idea what he is for without an emergency.
recruits.greeting: I've walked into worse than this. Stay behind me and breathe. — No, actually breathe, out loud, so I can hear you doing it.

background_sections.before: A truck, a crew, and the specific silence in a cab on the way back from one that went badly.
background_sections.adjustment:
Easiest first year, hardest second, and he can tell you the exact week it turned.

There was no crew to notice, which was most of the problem. The sun answers him the way a good crew does — when called, and all at once — and he has stopped pretending that is not most of what is holding him together.
background_sections.now:
Ashenvale East, working the ground around Grom's Rest where the corruption burns out of people slowly and nobody has a protocol for it.

He has written one. It is four lines long, it is wrong in at least one place, and it is the only one that exists.
background_sections.forward:
A crew. Not companions. Rostered, trained, able to do it without him standing there.

He is aware this is the same thing he wanted on Earth and never got, and that the reason he never got it was that he kept going in alone. Knowing that has not yet changed what he does when the call comes.

He has not looked for anybody. There are two kids in Grom's Rest whose mother did not come out of the corruption, and he has been in that village for fourteen months, and every single person who knows him can see what has happened except him.

recruits.name: Marta Kowalski
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years blasting in the Sudbury basin: drill the pattern, charge it, wire it, walk a long way back, and then the part everybody else finds exciting and she finds arithmetic. She has never once been surprised by a bang and holds a low opinion of people who are — being surprised means somebody measured wrong, and somebody measuring wrong is how you lose a hand. She regards the Integration as an inconvenience that improved her supply situation and will not be moved off that position by anybody, including people who have tried.
recruits.greeting: Fire in the hole. Yes, I say it every time. No, I am not going to stop. — Back up. Further. Further than that, you are not made of stone.

background_sections.before:
A pattern, a wire, and a long walk back. Her father did the same job in the same basin and told her not to.

*Nie mój cyrk, nie moje małpy* — not my circus, not my monkeys. She says it about every part of the job that is not the charge itself.
background_sections.adjustment:
Pressed hard, she will concede exactly one difficulty, and she concedes it like a woman paying a parking fine.

The charges here come with intent. A fuse that wants something is not a fuse, it is a colleague, and she had nineteen years of habits built on materials that had no opinions. She has rebuilt the habits. She remains annoyed.
background_sections.now:
Boulder Lode Mine: a Venture Co. claim dug badly by people in a hurry, which she describes as the most natural working environment of her life.

She is re-shoring the sections the goblins left. Partly so she can get at the back of it. Mostly because it offends her.

There is a goblin on her shift called Nix who is nineteen, reckless, and going to lose a hand. She has started checking his pattern before he fires it. She has not examined why a woman with no children of her own is doing this and would be furious if anybody suggested a reason.
background_sections.forward:
A face nobody has shot before, and the time to open it properly rather than fast.

Also — and she is serious about this — one goblin engineer saying out loud, in front of a witness, that her pattern is better than theirs. She has waited two years and is prepared to wait considerably longer.

recruits.name: Callum Reid
recruits.backstory: Sixteen years keeping reptiles at a Queensland sanctuary: taipans, death adders, and the constant low-grade public-relations work of explaining that the animal is not malicious, it is frightened and you are enormous. He has been envenomated more often than any person should be and files all of it under professional development. His forearms are a map of the learning curve. His adjustment here was almost entirely physical and took about eighteen months of being very unwell on purpose, a method he does not recommend and will not describe in detail to anybody who might copy him.
recruits.greeting: Don't worry about the scorpion. Mate, honestly — it's the least dangerous thing on me.

background_sections.before: A sanctuary, a hook, and school groups who all wanted to know the same thing about the same snake.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eighteen months of deliberate poisoning, conducted alone, documented badly.

What he got out of it is a working relationship with things that kill people — the same relationship he had before, with better participants.
background_sections.now:
The Southern Barrens, within reach of the Wailing Caverns, where the serpents are a great deal more than serpents and hold a clear view about intruders.

He goes in regularly and comes out reliably. The one time he brought something out alive the Crossroads made him promise not to do it again, and he promised.
background_sections.forward:
He would like to be bitten by whatever is at the bottom of the Caverns and survive it, and he is entirely aware of how that sentence reads.

His defensible position, which he will defend: the thing that bites back is the thing that trusts you, and he has not yet met the animal that was not worth the conversation.

recruits.name: Emre Kaya
recruits.backstory: He started at nine, sent to fetch a stuck deadbolt for an uncle in the old bazaar, and discovered that every lock is a short conversation with somebody who is not in the room. Thirty doors a week for most of his life after that. He was never a thief — he was the man you called when you had locked yourself out of your own livelihood, and he knew the inside of more businesses in that quarter than their owners did. Here the work is identical except that once, while he was still working the mechanism, the thing behind the door asked him a question. He got the door open. He has never said whether he answered it.
recruits.greeting: A locked door is a conversation. Let me do the talking — you will interrupt, everyone interrupts, and then it takes twice as long.

background_sections.before:
A roll of picks his uncle left him, and a quarter where four crafts died in his own lifetime while he watched.

*Bir kapı kapanır, bir kapı açılır* — one door closes, another opens. His mother said it constantly. He thought it was a proverb about God until he was about thirty and decided it was a proverb about him.
background_sections.adjustment:
None worth the name. A bigger bazaar with worse customers, and he has been perfectly content for three years, which makes him unusual company in any room of transplants.

The uncomfortable part, which he will concede if pressed by somebody he likes: he is content partly because the shop is gone and so is everyone who would have wanted it kept open a certain way. He did not lose a family. He lost an obligation, and he has been lighter since, and he does not say that where other transplants can hear it.
background_sections.now:
Eastern Hillsbrad, in the country around Durnholde — a keep full of doors built by people who were serious about them.

He is not looting it. He is reading it: which lock came first, which were added after somebody got in, and therefore where somebody got in.
background_sections.forward:
The one that beats him. He has not met it and has started to worry that he never will, which is a strange thing to be frightened of and he is frightened of it anyway.

Less romantically: an apprentice. The trade dies with him otherwise, and he has already watched that happen four times to men he knew.

recruits.name: Bakyt Asanov
recruits.backstory: Third generation, forty winters with a golden eagle on his arm in the mountains of Kyrgyzstan. He has never owned an animal in his life — he has been trusted by one, which he will tell you is an entirely different arrangement and a far more demanding one. His eagle did not come through with him. That is the whole of his first year, and he has said perhaps six sentences about it in three years.
recruits.greeting: She chooses who she flies for. For now she says you are acceptable. Do not look pleased, it is not a compliment yet.

background_sections.before:
A ridge, a glove, and his father's bird buried beside his own first bird in the same ground.

He goes up there in spring. He has never explained why and nobody has ever needed him to.

His sons were grown and gone and are grown and gone here as well — both alive, both west, both visited twice. That is a better outcome than almost anybody he knows has had and he is careful never to say so out loud in company.
background_sections.adjustment:
What he did instead of grieving in any manner anybody recognised was walk into the nearest high country and sit, for most of a season, until something came down to look at him.

He has not named it. Naming it would be presumptuous, he says, which is the closest thing to a religious statement he has ever made in front of a witness.
background_sections.now:
The Hillsbrad foothills, which are not his mountains and are near enough to work with. He hunts the high ground above Tarren Mill where the ridges run the right way.

A bird and a man still hunt the same ridge and the bird is still in charge. That part survived the crossing intact, which he regards as the only piece of luck he has had.
background_sections.forward:
Getting a young one through its first winter. Everything else is detail and he will not be drawn further.

He has started watching the Aspen Wilderness on the horizon, because it is tall and cold and the right shape, and a man who has spent forty winters on a mountain can tell from a long way off whether a mountain is any good.

recruits.name: Henrik Dahl
recruits.backstory: Twenty years of ice cores out of Tromsø: drill, extract, log, and read ten thousand years of weather out of a tube of frozen water. He has stood on a plateau at forty below and recorded in his notes that it was a good day, and he meant it without irony. Ice is the most honest archive there is — it cannot be edited, only lost. Here the frost answers him as a colleague rather than a subject, and he found that professionally awkward for most of a year, because twenty years of method assume the thing you are studying is not studying you. He has rewritten his own protocols three times and is not satisfied with the third.
recruits.greeting: Cold is only slow information. Let us see what it has to say. — You may complain while we work, that is permitted.

background_sections.before: A drill, a hut, and six months of dark a year that he has described as the only sensible way to divide a calendar.
background_sections.adjustment: Methodological, and ongoing. In every other respect he is precisely the man he was, which his colleagues on Earth would not have found surprising in the least.
background_sections.now:
The Frostward Descent, under Hillsbrad, where the ice is older than anything on the surface and has begun giving things back.

He is reading it the only way he knows how: layer by layer, slowly, writing everything down. He has found four things so far. He has reported two.
background_sections.forward:
The bottom of that ice, and the oldest layer in it.

He believes it is older than this world's own account of itself. He has told nobody that part. He is a careful man and would like considerably more evidence before saying something that size out loud.

recruits.name: Anjali Nair
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years as an agronomist in Kerala, teaching smallholders to keep a field alive through a monsoon that had stopped keeping the old calendar. Her career was patience and arithmetic: this much mulch, that much shade, wait. The thanks, when it came, came from somebody's mother rather than anybody official. Here the soil gives back with interest and she did not trust it for a year — not a spiritual crisis, a professional one, because nineteen years had taught her that fast growth is a loan. She has now watched a full cycle complete without collapsing and she has revised the model. Carefully. With a note about sample size.
recruits.greeting: Everything heals if you stop poking it. Mostly. — Stand still. I said still, that is not still.

background_sections.before:
Demonstration plots, a scooter, and a notebook per village.

She was never anybody's expert. She was the woman who came back in the second year, which turned out to be the whole job.
background_sections.adjustment: A year of refusing to believe the yield.
background_sections.now:
Ashenvale West, among people who have tended this forest for longer than her country has had that name, and who were not expecting to be taught anything by a transplant.

They were right. She is not teaching. She is doing what she did in Kerala — sitting with the people who actually work the ground and asking what has stopped working.

Her husband and both daughters are in Astranaar, eleven days away, and have been for two years. She visits in the dry months. Everyone assumes she will move there eventually and she has let everyone assume it, including them.
background_sections.forward:
One bad season, handled well. Anybody can grow things in a good season.

Her healing is mostly patience, and she is increasingly aware that this is also her entire personality, and that she has no intention of doing anything about it.

recruits.name: Hana Tamihana
recruits.backstory: Fourteen summers of black sand and heavy water on the Waikato coast, and a rip that took somebody every few years no matter how many signs went up. She has pulled a great many people out and she remembers the two she did not, by name, including the one whose family still sends her nothing. She was nineteen when she arrived here into a world of people with whole careers behind them, and she spent a year being treated as the kid, which is the part that actually stung.
recruits.greeting: Stay on my left and don't argue with it. Water's not your mate and it's not your enemy, it's just honest — people drown because they try to negotiate.

background_sections.before:
The beach. Patrol, flags, and a tower her uncle had sat in before her.

The water taught her the only thing about water that matters and she has never needed a second lesson.
background_sections.adjustment:
Less to unlearn than most, and she will tell you flatly that is luck and not merit.

The tide spirits read her the way she reads a break — take what is offered, give back, never turn your back on it — and the whole arrangement was legible inside a week. Her real adjustment was social, and it took three years.
background_sections.now:
The Hillsbrad coast. Colder and greyer than home, same undertow.

She has been teaching the fishing families to read it. Two of them listen. One of those two has stopped losing nets, which has done more for her standing in Southpoint than anything she could have said about herself.
background_sections.forward:
A bigger sea. She says it lightly and she is not joking: there is a coast west of Ashenvale where the water apparently does something nobody can describe properly to her, and that is now a problem she owns.

She is also working west because west is where the transit hub is, and the hub is where the lists go up. She checks them. She was nineteen and her whole family was at the beach that morning, which means they are somewhere, and nineteen-year-olds do not accept *somewhere* the way older people have learned to.

recruits.name: Kesten Ambrose
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years a monumental mason in Aberdeen, cutting letters into granite for people who had died. It is a trade with one unforgiving rule and he will give it to you unprompted: the stone does not care how you felt about the deadline. He cut names for families who could not pay and never mentioned it to anyone. He walked down the Alterac fissure in the first year, before there was a path worn into the lip, not looking for safety but for the only people he had met who were also writing things down. The Codex did not turn him away and did not quite take him in. They gave him a catalogue number — the most anybody has ever formally given him — and he has never once objected.
recruits.greeting: Entry four hundred and six. That is me, not a thing I found. You get used to it.

background_sections.before:
A yard, a mallet, and a good tradesman's reputation in a city that did not otherwise notice him. He was, by any measure that matters, fairly lonely.

He has not described it that way out loud. He would if asked directly.

There was nobody to lose. That is the quiet thing about him and it is why a catalogue number landed the way it did: it is the first time anything has recorded that he is here.
background_sections.adjustment: He arrived with his hands and nothing else, which for a man of his trade is the entire inventory.
background_sections.now:
Kael's Bastion. Entry eleven thousand and something, the only line in the whole index that is a person.

He cuts their runes now — the deep ones, in the columns, the ones that have to outlast the people who ordered them. Same trade, same rule, considerably better stone.
background_sections.forward:
He would like to know whether the number is loyalty or the closest thing to a headstone anyone has ever offered him.

Three years and he has not decided. He suspects the Codex have not decided either, and that this makes it the most honest relationship in the cavern.

recruits.name: Tarek Mansour
recruits.backstory: Eleven years in a conservation lab under the Egyptian Museum: linen, consolidant, and a scalpel ground thinner than a scalpel should be. He was the man who said no to the exhibition schedule, which made him unpopular with everybody except the objects. The work he does now is the same work — standing between the public and the artefact and being extremely boring about it. The artefact is whoever is behind him.
recruits.greeting: I take the front. Understand what that means — when it goes wrong you do not come back for me, you finish what you were doing. People get this backwards and then there are two of us on the floor instead of one.

background_sections.before:
A basement, a loupe, and things older than any country he could name.

He was good at the part of the job that is simply refusing to hurry.
background_sections.adjustment:
He was carrying a tray down a corridor and he arrived still holding it. He set it down on grass, very carefully, before he looked up.

He has said since that the setting down is the only part of those three years he is proud of.
background_sections.now:
Eastern Ashenvale, among ruins older than the Integration that are being taken apart faster than anyone is recording them.

He stands at the front of whoever is walking, and in the lulls he writes down what the carvings said before the saws reach them. He is losing the race and he knows the exact rate.
background_sections.forward:
The ruins recorded properly. Not at a run. With somebody holding a lamp.

He has asked nobody, because he knows exactly how it sounds to stand in a war and request a note-taker.

recruits.look: Egyptian man in his late 30s, medium height and thickening at the middle, close-cropped black hair receding at the temples, heavy brows, a careful unhurried face. Dark leather tank harness over a padded gambeson in sand and oxblood, a broad round shield, a short heavy blade kept sheathed. A pair of white cotton conservator's gloves folded through his belt, laundered grey.

recruits.name: Fiona Strachan
recruits.backstory: She counts the people around her before she moves. She did it in a crane cab a hundred and twenty miles off Aberdeen, twelve on and twelve off, three weeks on the water and three at home, and she does it here, and she will do it whether or not anybody has asked her to. Moving something enormous over the heads of people who trust you, in bad weather, without ever once being interesting about it. Nobody clapped on the deck either.
recruits.greeting: Front. Aye. Standing still while something hits me isn't the hard part of my day and never was.

background_sections.before: The cab. She was good and she was known for it, in the small way a crane operator is known.
background_sections.adjustment:
A fortnight of looking up for a load that was not there. That passed.

The counting did not.
background_sections.now:
The cape road and the drowned terraces below Zul'Kundaraz, where the Saltscale come up out of water she does not trust an inch.

She has made herself the person who goes in first. The Bay finds that useful and does not pay extra for it.
background_sections.forward:
A reason to be somewhere specific rather than wherever the work is.

She has started saying this out loud, which for her is enormous, and she has noticed that nobody has yet offered her one.

recruits.look: Scottish woman in her mid 40s, tall and square-built, sandy-grey hair cut short and shoved back, weather-ruined face, pale eyes set deep. Blackened mail over a long coat in slate and rust, a heavy tower shield slung at her back, a flanged mace at her hip. A yellow offshore survival-suit whistle still clipped to her collar on a fraying lanyard.

recruits.name: Pavlo Hryn
recruits.backstory: Twenty-six years of cab and road and radio out of Lviv, mostly alone, mostly at night, across borders that changed under him more than once. He is not frightened of the dark and he is not frightened of distance. He is extremely frightened of stopping. The Bay has not noticed this and he has no plans to mention it. He walked for nine days after he arrived before he spoke to anybody, and he describes those as the most normal nine days he has had in thirty years.
recruits.greeting: I stand in front. You do not have to like me, you do not have to talk. Talking is what crew wants from a man and is the one thing I never learned on road.

background_sections.before:
A flat in Lviv he was in for maybe sixty nights a year. A wife for eleven of those years and then not.

He knew every bad bend between Lviv and Rotterdam by the feel of the wheel, and he could not tell you the colour of his own kitchen.
background_sections.adjustment: Nine days of walking, and then a job, and then another one.
background_sections.now:
Silverpine, in the lower rings where the lamps are furthest apart, taking the work nobody else wants down a flooded corridor.

He is at his best in a place with one way out. He has never examined why.
background_sections.forward:
Stopping. He does not know how to begin and he is aware that is not a thing a grown man should need help with.

He has started asking what it costs to keep a room by the month. He has asked four people. He has not taken a room.

recruits.look: Ukrainian man in his early 50s, huge through the shoulders and gone soft over it, shaved head, grey stubble, a nose broken long ago and badly set. Dark iron plate with a black tabard and a greatshield, faint ember-red light in the seams of the gauntlets. A steel thermos flask, dented and lidless, strapped where a water flask should go.

recruits.name: Jun-seo Park
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years welding hulls in a Ulsan drydock, mostly night shift because the steel moves less when it is cool, inside compartments that had not been opened yet — where a man watches the gas meter and his own two hands and nothing else exists. He is unbothered by confined dark places and openly puzzled that anybody treats this as a personality rather than a work history.
recruits.greeting: People hear the spec and expect something from me. A mood, maybe. I welded ships. I will stand where the hit lands, you will work behind me, and that is all this is.

background_sections.before:
Two apprentices he liked and one he could not teach.

He still thinks about the third one. He has never been able to work out whether the failure was the boy's or his, and he has had nineteen years and a world ending to consider it.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived with the shade down and the arc still burned into his eyes.

He has said the worst part was how quiet it was.
background_sections.now:
Central Stranglethorn: the arena apron and the Veilfall's dry shoulder, taking the hits for whoever is working behind him.

He has no interest in the drums at all and finds the betting faintly embarrassing.
background_sections.forward:
To teach somebody something properly — start to finish, and have it hold.

He has not found anyone who will stand still long enough, and he is starting to suspect the problem is not them.

His wife and his mother are both in Ratchet and both well, and he sends money and does not visit, and when asked why he says the work is here. The work is not especially here. He cannot explain the rest of it and has stopped attempting to.

recruits.look: South Korean man in his early 40s, wiry and slightly stooped, black hair shot with grey and flattened by a helmet, a long patient face, deep smile lines he does not use often. Grey-black mail with a hooded mantle and a scythe-headed polearm carried butt-down. A welder's flip-up shade, cracked across one lens, pushed up on his forehead.

recruits.name: Minh Tran
recruits.backstory: Fourteen years of other people's pianos in Hanoi — houses, schools, and one concert hall that could not afford him and had him anyway. He could hear a unison go sour through a closed door and across a courtyard. He heals on the same principle: a beat early, while the thing is still cheap to fix. People find it unnerving for about a week and indispensable thereafter, and he has learned to wait out the week without defending himself.
recruits.greeting: I will keep you standing. Better two seconds before you need it than one second after — so if I move and you felt nothing yet, this is the work going correctly. It is not me wasting your time.

background_sections.before:
A fork, a wrench, a bicycle, and a city full of instruments that were nobody's priority.

He was not a musician and did not pretend to be. He made it possible for musicians, which he has always considered the better half of the arrangement.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived holding a tuning fork, in a world with no piano in it.

He admits the first year was mostly grief for an instrument, and he is aware of how that sounds next to what other people lost. He says it anyway, because it is true, and because pretending otherwise would be a kind of lying he does not do.
background_sections.now:
The Northern Barrens road, where there is always somebody being carried in off the sand. He has become the man the caravan masters send for before a fight rather than after one.

He still strikes the fork when he is thinking. The orcs have stopped remarking on it.
background_sections.forward:
Something built on this world that is worth tuning. He has been listening to the Zul'Marosh vinespeakers' knot-cords and suspects they are music, and has told nobody for fear of being wrong about it in front of people whose thing it is.

The other project is a list. Every transplant he treats gets asked three questions before he lets them go, and the answers go in a book he has been keeping since the first year. Four hundred names in it now. None of them are his wife's and the book is not for him any more — people have started coming to read it.

recruits.look: Vietnamese man in his late 30s, slight and neat, black hair parted and kept flat, round wire glasses, an attentive head-tilted way of standing. Pale blue and bone-white robes with long cuffs and a brass-ringed orrery at the belt, a slim staff with a slow-turning ring at its head. A tuning fork on a cord round his neck, the tines worn bright.

recruits.name: Alonso Vega
recruits.backstory: A hot shop off a side street in Guadalajara, his father's before it was his: three benches and a furnace they fed in shifts so it never once went cold. He made vases nobody needed and one window for a church that is still standing. Fire was a tool you respected rather than a thing you feared, so healing with it was not a leap for him at all. Everybody else finds it a leap, and he has given up on the explanation.
recruits.greeting: Yes, it is fire. It was always fire — twenty years I kept something alive at eleven hundred degrees. Hold still. It will feel like standing too close to an oven, and then it will feel like nothing.

background_sections.before: The furnace. Twenty years of it, and it never went out, not once, including the week his father died.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived with a blowpipe and a gather still on the end of it, and watched the glass go solid in the grass because there was no annealer anywhere in the world any more.

It cracked as it cooled. He kept the pieces for a year and then stopped.
background_sections.now:
The Veilfall basin and the arena apron, where burns come in steadily and most healers flinch at them.

He does not flinch at burns. He is also the only source of flat glass within four days' walk, which he finds extremely funny and nobody else does.
background_sections.forward:
A furnace. He has picked the spot, worked out the clay, and started badgering Booty Bay about sand, and he is entirely serious about every part of it.

The sand is from the south. So is the rest of it — his daughters are somewhere below the range, he is nearly certain, because that is where the hub for Guadalajara came down. A furnace is a thing you build when you are planning to be somewhere a long time. He is aware of what he is telling himself.

recruits.look: Mexican man in his mid 40s, broad and short, thick black hair pushed back off a high forehead, forearms shiny with old burn scars, a wide easy face. Deep orange and ash-grey robes cut short at the sleeve for the heat, a censer-headed staff trailing warm light. A pair of smoked-glass glassblower's goggles hung at his throat.

recruits.name: Delroy Beckford
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years of nights in a bakery on Spanish Town Road, in at eleven and out at seven, measuring by hand and by feel. He knew the weather by how the dough behaved and the regulars by what they bought. A brew is a dough with different patience. He treats a wounded party exactly like an order going out at dawn: everybody gets something, nobody waits long, and the complaining is part of the process.
recruits.greeting: Sit. Drink that. No, I'm not telling you what's in it, you wouldn't thank me. Thirty-one years I fed a city its breakfast and not one of them ever asked what was in the bread either.

background_sections.before: The night shift. He has never in his life been awake at the same hours as everybody else and has never regarded that as a sacrifice.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived at four in the morning his time, which is the only reason, he says, that he was not asleep when it happened.

He says it like a joke. It is not entirely a joke and he knows which parts are which.
background_sections.now:
Booty Bay, on the lower gallery, where the pier work breaks people steadily and the Baron does not care.

He works nights out of habit and has a following among the bruisers, who pretend not to be queueing.

Every ship that ties up gets the same three names asked of it. The Bay thinks this is a charming habit of the old baker's. It is not a habit. It is a system, it is the reason he took a pitch on the gallery and not up the hill, and in three years it has produced one maybe.
background_sections.forward:
An oven, and then an apprentice, in that order, and he has made it clear he will not be hurried on either count.

He has been offered a share in a Bay kitchen twice and turned it down twice, for reasons he gives freely and which nobody finds convincing.

recruits.look: Jamaican man in his early 50s, tall and lean with a slight permanent stoop, grey locs tied back, a long lined face that goes from grave to delighted with no warning. Leather and woven-grass healer's gear in moss and bone, a cauldron-bowl slung at the hip and a short paddle-like stave. A floury canvas apron, folded and tied at the waist, never quite clean.

recruits.name: Imelda Salonga
recruits.backstory: Fish on a Navotas quay from five in the morning, boxing in the evenings, the same six streets her whole life, and a mother who called the boxing a phase for nineteen years. Ten fights a year and she won more than she lost. Her healing is not gentle and does not look like healing — she hits things and her people get better — and it took the Vine Road about a week to stop asking and roughly a year to stop watching her sideways while it worked.
recruits.greeting: I know how it looks. Stay behind me and watch — when I land one, you will feel it. I could never explain this in my own language either, so.

background_sections.before:
A stall, a gym above a tyre shop, and hands she wrapped herself because nobody else did it tight enough.

Her mother called the boxing a phase for nineteen years and then turned up at Freewind Post two summers ago, on a goblin barge, having asked after her in four languages all the way down the coast. She lives in the Post now. She still calls it a phase.
background_sections.adjustment: She arrived at market hour with her hands already wrapped, which she has decided to call luck and which nobody has been able to talk her out of.
background_sections.now:
Freewind Post, where the tauren walk the lifts and the drop does the rest, and the injured come in steadily all week.

The Post asks for her by name without being able to say what she is. She still wraps her hands before anything else, including breakfast.
background_sections.forward:
She has started asking around the arena whether anybody here fights properly — rules, a count, somebody keeping time.

The answers so far have been enthusiastic and have not been about that at all, and she is getting tired of explaining the difference.

recruits.look: Filipina woman in her mid 30s, compact and visibly strong through the shoulders, black hair in a short practical knot, flat nose, a scar through one eyebrow. Mail and green hide cut for movement, wrapped fists, no shield and no staff at all. A pair of soft hand-wraps from a boxing gym, washed to grey, rewound every morning.

recruits.name: Tomas Havel
recruits.backstory: Eighteen years up in the grid in Prague, on tour and in houses, at four in the morning, hanging weight over the heads of people who would never once look up. The job was leverage, timing, and never being the reason something fell. He swings a two-hander like a man who has spent his life moving heavy things through small gaps, and he has still not drawn it on anything worse than a training post, which he is in no hurry to change.
recruits.greeting: Big sword, lots of room. Tell me where you want me standing before it starts, not during. I have worked with people who shout during. I did not enjoy any of them.

background_sections.before: A bad shoulder from a truss in 2014 that he worked through because the show was that night. It still tells him when the weather is turning and he still works through it.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived forty feet up, which should have killed him, and he has never once managed to tell that story without it coming out as a brag.

He has given up trying to fix the delivery and now just gets it over with early.
background_sections.now:
Fenris Isle and whatever scaffolding he can reach, because people here build fast and tie off badly and he physically cannot walk past it.

He is paid in food and the occasional argument.
background_sections.forward:
Something that stays up.

He has been looking at the way this city holds its roofs on with an expression the orcs find difficult to read and have decided not to ask about.

There was a woman in Prague and he had not asked her yet, and three years is long enough that he has started describing her in the past tense without noticing, which his friends have noticed.

recruits.look: Czech man in his early 40s, rangy and long-armed, dark hair cut short, a thin face with a permanent squint from years of looking up into lights. Battered plate with the pauldrons stripped off for reach, a two-handed sword worn across the back. A steel carabiner clipped to his belt loop, scratched to bare metal.

recruits.name: Eino Virtanen
recruits.backstory: Eleven years welding pipeline in Lapland and then in colder places, fourteen days on and fourteen off, in weather where a mistake takes a hand off at the wrist. He talks about as much as the job required, which is almost not at all. He fights with both hands because he has never been able to pick a favourite and has stopped treating that as something to resolve.
recruits.greeting: Two axes. You do not need to tell me twice. If I stop talking, it is because there is nothing to say. It is not that something is wrong.

background_sections.before:
A cabin he built badly on purpose, because he wanted something to keep improving. A brother he telephoned every Sunday without fail for nine years.

He has no idea whether the brother is alive. He stopped constructing scenarios about it, which took two years and was deliberate work. What he did not stop is the other thing: every convoy out of Grom'gol gets the same question in the same four words, and he has asked it so many times that the drivers answer before he finishes.
background_sections.adjustment: He arrived in rotation gear with a flask of coffee that stayed hot for the first hour. That is the detail he always mentions, every time, and he has never once gone past it.
background_sections.now:
The Vine Road and the cutline fork, taking whatever the Grom'gol convoys will pay for and spending almost none of it.

He is liked considerably more than he has noticed and would be embarrassed to find out.
background_sections.forward:
The cabin again. Properly badly.

He has been pricing timber out of Grom'gol with a seriousness nobody expected from him and which two separate traders have found unnerving.

recruits.look: Finnish man in his late 30s, enormous and pale, red-blond hair and a thick beard, small light eyes, a face that gives away nothing. Heavy hide and fur over bare arms, a hand axe in each fist. A length of orange pipeline marking tape knotted round one bicep, faded to salmon.

recruits.name: Ziad Haddad
recruits.backstory: Nine years behind a desk in rooms with no windows, four nights a week, reading a crowd in the dark and riding the exact moment it turned. He could tell you what a room was going to want eight bars before it wanted it. He fights on the same instinct and he is good enough at it that it has started to worry people who like him. He knows precisely what bargain he made. He declines to discuss it in a way that is almost charming, and the almost is doing a great deal of work.
recruits.greeting: I go in first and I come out fast. Do not follow me in — that is not modesty, you will genuinely be in my way.

background_sections.before: A flat above a bakery in Mar Mikhael and a city that had already taught him what it costs to stay somewhere you love.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived at two in the morning with the set still running.

The silence afterwards is the thing he has never been able to describe properly, and he has tried, to four people, in two languages.
background_sections.now:
The Bloodsail shallows and the wrecks off Jaguero Spit, where he is paid well and asked nothing.

The green in his eyes has got stronger this last year. He has started wearing a hood and has told everybody it is the sun.
background_sections.forward:
Whether what he took can be given back.

He has asked two people. Both laughed. He has stopped asking and has not stopped wanting to know.

He took it in the first place to get south. That is the part he does not discuss and the part that explains everything else: the Beirut hub is below the range, his mother and both sisters were in the city, and the pass kills ordinary people. He is no longer an ordinary person and he is still on this side of it.

recruits.look: Lebanese man in his early 30s, slim and quick, black curls kept long on top, a sharp handsome face he is aware of, dark eyes with a faint green cast now. Purple-black leathers cut close with a half-cape, twin curved blades, a thin fel shimmer on the edges. A single foam earplug on a cord, tucked behind his collar.

recruits.name: Pieter Malan
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years keeping a provincial rugby ground outside Bloemfontein — grass, lines, drainage, and Saturdays spent watching other people use what he had made. He knew every soft patch on that pitch and could give you the drainage history of all of it. He is a tank by trade and refuses to play like one, on the stated grounds that he has done quite enough standing about, and the heat in his voice when he says it surprises people who have only met the cheerful version.
recruits.greeting: I have a shield and I am going to hit you with it. Twenty-two years I watched other people run onto a field I cut. I am not standing at the back of anything again.

background_sections.before: A mower, a line marker, a shed, and a wife who ran the clubhouse bar and could fill it on a Tuesday.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived on a Saturday morning with the lines half cut.

He says the worst of it is not knowing whether anybody finished them. He says that instead of the other thing, which is that his wife arrived in the Barrens and took eleven months to reach him, and that she is quieter now than she was and he does not know what happened in those eleven months because she has never told him.
background_sections.now:
Northern Tanaris, out along the salt road, in the thick of it and loudly.

He has made himself popular in every camp between here and the coast and mildly notorious with anybody who has ever tried to organise him.
background_sections.forward:
A patch of flat ground and permission to cut it.

He is aware this is not what anybody expects a man of his size and volume to say, and he says it anyway, to anybody who asks, immediately.

recruits.look: South African man in his mid 40s, heavy and sunburnt, thinning blond hair, a flat pugnacious face, forearms like a man who has swung things for a living. Dull gold plate worn open at the throat, a one-handed mace and a shield he uses offensively. A groundsman's folding knife on a belt loop, handle worn pale.

recruits.name: Esteban Ruiz
recruits.backstory: A radiographer's job is standing a person in front of something harmful in precisely the right dose, and he did it for twenty years in Rosario without once getting it wrong. He reasoned his way into the Bloodmage path from there and the reasoning is sound. The ledger is the problem. He keeps one on his own use, in the same hand he kept the exposure logs in, and he has worked out that there is nobody on this world qualified to check his arithmetic. He is handling that considerably less well than he lets on.
recruits.greeting: I use my own blood — before you say the thing everyone says. Twenty years I calculated exposure for a living. I am the only one in this camp who writes down what it costs him.

background_sections.before: Imaging suites, lead aprons, the same three corridors, and a daughter studying in Córdoba whose last message to him was about a bus.
background_sections.adjustment:
He kept the apron. Wore it for the first year here, over everything, in a climate it had no business in, and did not explain himself to anybody who asked.

It fell apart eventually. He has the collar.
background_sections.now:
Orgrimmar, doing the work the city's own healers will not, which in a city this size is steady trade.

The ledger is on the table. Nobody has ever asked to see it. He would hand it over immediately.
background_sections.forward:
Somebody qualified to check the numbers. There is no such person and he has known it for two years. He asks anyway, of every scholar who comes through Orgrimmar, in a tone that makes it sound like a formality.

He asks them something else too, afterwards, when they are already leaving: whether they have heard of a young woman, Argentine, studying, would be twenty-six now. He has asked two hundred and forty-one people. He knows the number because he writes those down as well.

recruits.look: Argentinian man in his late 30s, medium build and going grey early at the front, neat beard, an unsettlingly calm bedside manner. Dark red leathers with a lamellar chest and a thin crimson blade, faint red light under the skin of his forearms. A radiation-badge dosimeter clipped at his collar, the window long since gone black.

recruits.name: Kiet Somsak
recruits.backstory: A locksmith's booth off a lane near Tha Phae, a scooter, and a reputation for being discreet — cutting keys for people who had locked themselves out and, occasionally, for people who had not. He is incurious about violence and extremely curious about mechanisms, and he will tell you that combination has kept him alive twice and employed continuously.
