recruits.greeting: I am quiet and I am not brave. These are two different things and both are worth paying for. Point me at what is shut.

background_sections.before: Opinions about every lock in the old city, and a favourite he would not name to anyone, including his wife, including under direct and repeated questioning.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived holding a customer's key.

He has kept it. Uncut, useless, three years, and he does not explain it.
background_sections.now:
The Abyssal Sands, where the buried doors are older than anything in Tanaris and were built by people who did not expect to be followed.

He opens them for whoever is paying and occasionally for nobody at all, and has already got further in than anyone has authorised.
background_sections.forward:
What the old stonework out here is hiding.

He has worked out that the answer is a very long way south, which has not deterred him in the slightest and has begun to alarm the two people who like him.

recruits.look: Thai man in his late 20s, small and economical in his movements, black hair cut short, a quiet watchful face, hands that are never still. Matte grey-green leathers with a soft hood down, a thin dagger at the small of the back. A brass key blank on a loop of wire at his belt, cut for nothing.

recruits.name: Stelios Dukas
recruits.backstory: Seventeen years running the library in a Corinth prison — a card catalogue he refused to digitise and a readership of four hundred men who were not supposed to matter. He knew every one of their borrowing histories and treated all of them as readers, which is the entire job and was never in the job description. The dead make perfect sense to him and he makes uncomfortable sense to them.
recruits.greeting: I keep records. You will find that less sinister than you expect and more useful than you think. Most of what walks here is only angry about being forgotten.

background_sections.before:
A room with high windows, a stamp, and four hundred men who came in for the warmth and left with something.

*Τα βιβλία δεν κρίνουν.* Books do not judge. He put it on the wall in his own hand and the governor made him take it down twice.
background_sections.adjustment: He arrived at the issue desk with the stamp in his hand, set it down on nothing, and picked it back up.
background_sections.now:
Glittervein, writing down what the dead in the deep workings remember, because nobody else is bothering and the seam is being cut out from under them.

The crews treat him as a harmless infestation and let him work, which is the most comfortable he has been in years.
background_sections.forward:
The catalogue finished, and left somewhere it will be read.

He is aware this is the only ambition he has ever had, and he has stopped apologising for the size of it.

Nobody is looking for him and he is not looking for anybody, and he has noticed that this makes him unusually good at sitting with people who are. He does not offer comfort. He writes the name down and reads it back, and more people have wept at that than he was prepared for.

recruits.look: Greek man in his early 50s, tall and gaunt, grey hair worn too long, a dry ironic face, half-moon reading glasses on a chain. Charcoal and bone robes with a high collar, a staff topped with a bound sheaf of pages. A librarian's date stamp, brass and wooden-handled, carried in a robe pocket.

recruits.name: Ratih Pranoto
recruits.backstory: Fifteen years measuring rivers for the Indonesian water service, mostly alone, mostly walking: the job of knowing where water will be next week. A motorbike, a notebook that was permanently wet, and the habit of being the only person who had walked the whole catchment. She reads a landscape the same way here, which is why she saw the tide line move before anybody in Booty Bay did, and why nobody believed her, and why she has stopped volunteering it.
recruits.greeting: I shoot from where the ground tells me to stand. If I say move — move. I have been right about water for fifteen years and I am right about this.

background_sections.before:
Gauging stations the length of Java, and a succession of officials who wanted the number to be different.

It was never different. She has a great deal of practice at this conversation.
background_sections.adjustment: She has not stopped surveying since the day she arrived, because there is an entire world of water here that nobody has written down.
background_sections.now:
The Shimmering Flats: a pan that was under water once and is not now, which is a thing nobody out there has written down and she cannot stop thinking about.

She is on good terms with exactly one tauren and no goblins at all.
background_sections.forward:
Somebody to write it down with her.

She has begun approaching strangers about this and she knows it is going badly. She cannot work out how to say *I need a second pair of hands for forty years of work* in a way that does not frighten people off, so she says it quickly and watches them leave.

She asks each of them one other thing first, which is whether they have been east. Her father was in Surabaya and Surabaya is not anywhere she has found yet.

recruits.look: Indonesian woman in her late 30s, slim and weathered, black hair in a tight braid, a direct unsmiling face, fine squint lines. Green and grey leathers with a quiver worn high, a long recurve bow. A brass river-gauge plate, stamped with marks, sewn flat onto her sleeve.

recruits.name: Kourosh Behzadi
recruits.backstory: Twelve years pricing mortality for a Tehran insurer: the work of establishing, very carefully, how likely a thing is. He finds arcane magic restful by comparison because for once the numbers hold still. He is the only person on this side of the mountains who has calculated his own odds and he will not tell anybody the figure, and the refusal is cheerful rather than grim, which people find worse.
recruits.greeting: I am going to stand back here and be extremely precise. You are welcome to be brave — somebody in a group should be, and it was never going to be the actuary.

background_sections.before:
Tables, reserving, a good office with a bad view, and a mother he telephoned on Fridays who thought the job was beneath him.

She was right that he was capable of more. She was wrong about what more would have meant.

He priced her odds in the second year, properly, with what was known about hub placement and survivorship, and then he stopped looking, because an actuary who does not act on his own table is not an actuary. He has never told anybody the figure. He has never told anybody there was a figure.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived mid-calculation and the first thing he did on this world was finish the sum.

He says that was not bravery, it was momentum, and he is irritated that people keep wanting it to be the other thing.
background_sections.now:
The Crystalline Underdark, where the lattice does something to arcane magic that nobody has characterised.

He is characterising it. The case is nearly full.
background_sections.forward:
There is no press, no journal and no readership, and he is writing it anyway — longhand, in a case he keeps dry.

He has told two people what is in it. Both changed the subject, and he recorded the date each time.

recruits.look: Iranian man in his late 30s, slender and slightly formal in his bearing, black hair neatly cut, close beard, a face that looks faintly amused at all times. Indigo and silver robes with precise geometric trim, a staff of nested rotating rings. A slim mechanical pencil, silver, clipped inside the collar of his robe.

recruits.name: Driss Alaoui
recruits.backstory: Sixteen years of nacelles and gearboxes and a van full of tools, on a ridge above Tangier where the wind did not stop between October and March. He could tell a bearing was going from the sound two weeks out. He already thought of weather as a colleague with moods, so the elements answering him back is, by his own account, the only genuinely new thing that has happened to him in his adult life — and he says that like a man reporting a result, not a revelation.
recruits.greeting: Sixteen years I climbed inside a machine to hear what the wind was doing to it. Now the wind tells me directly. I have not yet decided if this is better.

background_sections.before: A tower, a harness, and the particular silence two hundred feet up when the blades are locked off and the whole thing is just metal in the wind.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived underground. Two hundred feet up inside a tower, and he came out of it underground.

He has never once found that funny and has stopped pretending to when other people do.
background_sections.now:
Freewind Post, on a mesa where the wind does not stop from one month to the next, which is the first thing since he arrived that has felt like his old ridge.

He is the only person up there who finds the weather legible rather than hostile, and the tauren have begun asking him what tomorrow is doing.
background_sections.forward:
Somewhere with weather, permanently. He has found it, which means the question he has been deferring for three years — what he actually does now — has finally arrived and he has no answer prepared.

He deferred it on purpose. For two of those years the answer was *keep moving west and keep asking*, and then he stopped in a place with good wind and the asking stopped with him, and he has not decided yet whether that was arriving or giving up.

recruits.look: Moroccan man in his mid 40s, lean and long-limbed, black hair greying at the temples under a wrapped headscarf, a narrow thoughtful face. Blue-grey mail and layered cloth with a totem stave and a horn at his belt, static lifting the loose ends of the scarf. A torque wrench, short and stubby, slung in a loop at his hip.

recruits.name: Marisol Quintero
recruits.backstory: Twenty-four years of her grandmother's funeral home on a street in Medellín, through a decade when the city gave them more than two women could carry. She knows the correct thing to say to anybody in any state, which is a skill that makes people in a party uneasy — she is the only one who will say the plain thing out loud about what just happened, and she says it kindly, and that is somehow worse. She is unshockable. She does not experience this as a virtue.
recruits.greeting: I have sat with more dead people than everybody on this quay put together. The shadow does not frighten me and it does not impress me. Shall we go?

background_sections.before:
The house on the corner, the cold room, her grandmother's ledger, and a street that knew to knock at the side door.

*Uno se acostumbra a todo menos a los niños.* You get used to everything except the children. She says it as a fact rather than a complaint.
background_sections.adjustment:
She was mid-wake when it happened, and what bothers her is not the arriving. It is that the family will have assumed the worst of her — that she walked out of a viewing, with their mother on the table, and did not come back.

There is no version of this where they ever find out otherwise. She has had three years to make peace with that and has made somewhat less than three years' progress.
background_sections.now:
Northern Silverpine, on the road where people stop being people and nobody marks the moment it happens.

She has started holding services. They are badly attended. The Forsaken have begun to notice that she does not flinch at them and does not pity them either, and a few of them have started turning up.
background_sections.forward:
The forgotten dead of this city are going to be named. All of them. She is entirely aware this is an absurd project and has allocated the rest of her life to it, which she considers a reasonable budget.

Her sister is in Brill. They found each other inside a year, which is luck on a scale that embarrasses her when other people are talking. They have not discussed the wake once in three years and Marisol has decided not to be the one who raises it.

recruits.look: Colombian woman in her mid 40s, small and very upright, black hair in a severe low bun, a composed face that reveals nothing at all. Deep violet and black robes with a plain white collar, a slim dark staff, shadow pooling at the hem. A pair of folding reading glasses in a hard case, carried in one sleeve.

notes: Recruitable companions - diverse classes, specs (FIXED), locations, and backgrounds. Each has distinctive NPC color for visibility. Backgrounds shortened to fit screen. Spec-locked recruitment identity. Recruits with "placed": false are fully authored (class, spec, background, art slot) but not yet standing anywhere in the world; "suggested_zone" is only a hint for when they are placed (several will go to the Eastern Kingdoms). A recruit's level matches the zone they are found in (Kyle, 2026-10-22), so nobody is a level 2 in a level 14 town.
